title: Sargam Theory Challenge
description: Test your knowledge of the seven swaras, their names, and their relationships.

tasks.title: The seven swaras
content: Indian music uses seven fundamental notes called swaras, collectively known as sargam (from Sa-Re-Ga-Ma).

items: Sa (Shadja) - the tonic, always fixed as your reference
Re (Rishabh) - the second note
Ga (Gandhar) - the third note
Ma (Madhyam) - the fourth note, the middle of the scale
Pa (Pancham) - the fifth note, always fixed relative to Sa
Dha (Dhaivat) - the sixth note
Ni (Nishad) - the seventh note, leading back to Sa

content.text: Sa and Pa are called 'achal' (immovable) swaras - they never change. The other five can be sharpened or flattened.

questions.prompt: Which two notes are 'achal' (immovable) and never change?

options.why: Re has komal (flat) and shuddha (natural) forms.

options.yes: Correct! Sa and Pa are the two fixed notes.

options.why: Both Ga and Ni have komal and shuddha forms.
Ma has shuddha and tivra (sharp) forms.

questions.prompt: What does the word 'sargam' come from?

options.text: The first four swaras: Sa Re Ga Ma
options.yes: Exactly! Sargam is shorthand for Sa-Re-Ga-Ma.

options.why: It is actually a concatenation of the first four note names.

options.text: The name of an ancient musician
options.why: It comes from the note names themselves.

options.text: The seven planets in Vedic astrology
options.why: While there are connections, the word is from Sa-Re-Ga-Ma.

hints: The mnemonic: Sa and Pa are the pillars. Everything else can move.
Sargam is like 'do-re-mi' - named after the notes themselves.

tasks.title: Name all seven swaras
content: Each swara has a full Sanskrit name. These names have been used for thousands of years and each carries meaning.

items: Sa = Shadja ('born of six' - the source from which the other notes are derived)
Re = Rishabh ('the bull' - strong and steady)
Ga = Gandhar ('fragrant' - sweet and melodious)
Ma = Madhyam ('the middle' - sits at the centre of the scale)
Pa = Pancham ('the fifth' - always a perfect fifth above Sa)
Dha = Dhaivat ('sustained' - resonant and full)
Ni = Nishad ('sitting down' - the note that settles back toward Sa)

questions.prompt: What is the full name of 'Sa'?
questions.no: It's Shadja - meaning 'born of six' because all other notes derive from it.

questions.prompt: What is the full name of 'Ma'?
questions.no: It's Madhyam - meaning 'the middle', as it sits at the centre of the scale.

questions.prompt: What is the full name of 'Pa'?
Which swara's name means 'the middle'?

options.why: Gandhar means 'fragrant'.

options.yes: Right! Madhyam means 'the middle' - it sits at the centre of the scale.

options.why: Pancham means 'the fifth'.
Dhaivat means 'sustained'.

hints: Shadja, Rishabh, Gandhar, Madhyam, Pancham, Dhaivat, Nishad.
Ma = Madhyam = Middle. Pa = Pancham = Fifth.

tasks.title: Komal and tivra
content: Five of the seven notes come in two flavours:

items: Komal (flat) - the lowered version, written in lowercase: r, g, d, n
Shuddha (natural) - the standard version, written in uppercase: R, G, D, N
Ma is special: its two forms are shuddha Ma (m) and tivra Ma (M, sharpened)

content: This gives us 12 notes in total - the same 12 pitches as Western music, but named and thought about differently.

questions.prompt: What is the sharpened form of Ma called?

options.why: Komal means flat. Ma's raised form has a different name.

options.yes: Correct! Tivra means sharp or intense.

options.why: Shuddha Ma is the natural (lower) form.
Ati is not the standard term for Ma's raised form.

questions.prompt: Which notes can take a komal (flat) form?

options.yes: Right! These four plus Ma (which uses tivra instead) are the vikrit swaras.

options.why: Sa is achal (immovable) and can never be flattened.
Sa and Pa are fixed. Ma uses tivra, not komal.
Ma does not take komal form - it uses tivra (sharp) instead.

questions.prompt: What is the Hindi/Sanskrit word for 'flat' in Indian music?
questions.no: The word is 'komal', meaning soft or tender.

hints: Remember: komal = lowered, shuddha = natural, tivra = sharpened.
Only Ma uses 'tivra' instead of a second 'shuddha'. All others use 'komal' for their lowered form.
The four komal notes: Re, Ga, Dha, Ni. Ma is the odd one out - it goes sharp, not flat.

tasks.title: The chromatic scale - all 12 pitches
content: When you count every shuddha, komal and tivra note, you get 12 distinct pitches in one octave. This is the same number as the 12 semitones in Western music.

items: S - Sa
r - komal Re
R - shuddha Re
g - komal Ga
G - shuddha Ga
m - shuddha Ma
M - tivra Ma
P - Pa
d - komal Dha
D - shuddha Dha
n - komal Ni
N - shuddha Ni

content.text: Notice that between Ga and Ma there is no extra note, and between Pa and Dha there is no extra note. These are the two 'half-step' gaps in the natural scale.

questions.prompt: How many total distinct pitches are there in one saptak (octave)?
Between which two shuddha notes is there NO komal or tivra note?

options.why: Komal Re sits between Sa and shuddha Re.
Komal Ga sits between shuddha Re and shuddha Ga.

options.yes: Correct! There is no note between shuddha Ga and shuddha Ma - it is a natural half step.

options.why: Tivra Ma sits between shuddha Ma and Pa.

questions.prompt: How many 'vikrit' (movable) swaras are there?

options.why: There are more than three movable notes.

options.yes: Right! Re, Ga, Ma, Dha, Ni are the five vikrit swaras.

options.why: Sa and Pa are achal (immovable), so not all seven are vikrit.
12 is the total number of pitches, not the number of movable swaras.

hints: Count: S, r, R, g, G, m, M, P, d, D, n, N = 12 pitches.
The two natural half steps: Ga-Ma and Ni-Sa (upper). No notes sit between them.
Vikrit means 'altered' - Re, Ga, Ma, Dha and Ni each have two forms.

tasks.title: Read sargam notation

items: Uppercase = shuddha (natural): S R G M P D N
Lowercase = komal (flat): r g d n, and tivra Ma is uppercase M
A dot below = lower octave (mandra saptak)
A dot above = upper octave (taar saptak)
No dot = middle octave (madhya saptak)

content: A dash (-) means hold the previous note for another beat. A comma separates notes within the same beat. A semicolon marks a bar line.

questions.prompt: In sargam notation, what does a lowercase 'g' mean?

options.why: Shuddha Ga is written as uppercase G.
Lower octave is shown with a dot below, not by case.

questions.prompt: Write the ascending sargam scale in capital letters, from Sa to Ni (e.g. S R G ...). Spaces between notes.
questions.answer: S R G M P D N
accept: S R G M P D N
s r g m p d n
questions.no: The seven shuddha swaras in order: S R G M P D N

questions.prompt: In notation, what does a dash (-) after a note mean?

options.why: A dash is about duration, not volume.

options.text: Hold the previous note for another beat
options.yes: Right! A dash sustains the note.

options.why: Silence is usually written differently.

options.text: Play the note in the lower octave
options.why: Octave is shown with dots, not dashes.

hints: The first letters: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni.
Uppercase = natural, lowercase = flat, dot above = high, dot below = low.
A dash (-) means 'keep holding that note'.

tasks.title: The three octaves
content: The bansuri's range spans roughly three octaves (saptaks). Each octave repeats the same seven swaras at a higher or lower pitch.

items: Mandra saptak (low octave) - deep, meditative, written with a dot below the note
Madhya saptak (middle octave) - the natural speaking range of the flute, no dot
Taar saptak (upper octave) - bright and piercing, written with a dot above the note

content: Most bansuri melodies live in the madhya saptak, dipping into mandra and reaching up to taar for expression.

content.text: The upper octave on a bansuri requires more air pressure (overblowing). The lower octave needs a gentle, relaxed breath.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the middle octave?
questions.no: It's the Madhya saptak - the middle octave where most melodies live.

questions.prompt: How is a note in the upper octave (taar saptak) written in sargam notation?

options.text: With a dot below the note
options.why: A dot below means the lower octave (mandra saptak).

options.text: With a dot above the note
options.yes: Right! A dot above means taar saptak.

options.why: Sargam notation uses dots for octave, not font style.

options.text: With an exclamation mark after it

questions.prompt: What is the Sanskrit name for the low octave?
questions.no: It's Mandra saptak - the low, deep octave.

hints: The three saptaks: Mandra (low), Madhya (middle), Taar (high).
Think: Mandra = mantra = deep and meditative. Taar = star = high and bright.

tasks.title: What is a thaat?
content: A thaat is a parent scale - a set of seven notes (one form of each swara) from which ragas are derived. The thaat system was organized by Pandit Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande in the early 20th century.
There are 10 thaats in Hindustani (North Indian) classical music. Each thaat:

items: Uses exactly seven notes - one version of each swara
Must include Sa and Pa (the two fixed notes)
Chooses shuddha or komal for Re, Ga, Dha, Ni
Chooses shuddha or tivra for Ma
Is named after its most famous raga

content.text: A thaat is a scale, not a raga. A raga has rules about ascending, descending, emphasis and mood. A thaat is just the set of notes.

questions.prompt: How many thaats are there in the Bhatkhande system?
questions.no: There are 10 thaats in the Bhatkhande system.

questions.prompt: What is a thaat?

options.text: A parent scale of seven notes from which ragas are derived
options.yes: Correct! A thaat is the foundation - the set of notes a raga draws from.

options.text: A rhythmic cycle used in Indian music
options.why: That would be a 'taal'. A thaat is about notes, not rhythm.

options.text: A specific raga with strict performance rules
options.why: A thaat is simpler - just a scale. A raga adds rules for melody and mood.
Ornaments are called 'alankar' or by specific names like meend, kan, murki.

hints: Thaat = parent scale. Raga = child melody built from that scale.
10 thaats, organized by Bhatkhande. Each named after its most famous raga.

tasks.title: Bilawal thaat - the natural scale
content: Bilawal is the most fundamental thaat. It uses all seven shuddha (natural) swaras - no komal or tivra notes at all.
Its notes: S R G m P D N (Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni - all in their natural form).
This is equivalent to the Western major scale (C major = C D E F G A B). If you can play the shuddha sargam ascending and descending, you already know Bilawal thaat.

content.text: Bilawal thaat is named after Raga Bilawal, which is traditionally performed in the morning and conveys a bright, serene mood.

content: The other nine thaats each change one or more notes from their shuddha form. For example, Kafi thaat uses komal Ga and komal Ni, giving it a minor-like feel.

questions.prompt: What makes Bilawal thaat special among the ten thaats?

options.why: While it may have ancient roots, its special status is about its notes.

options.text: It uses all shuddha (natural) swaras - no komal or tivra
options.yes: Exactly! Bilawal is the 'default' scale - all notes in their natural form.

options.why: Every thaat uses all seven swaras.

options.text: It can only be played at night
options.why: Bilawal is traditionally a morning raga.

questions.prompt: Which Western scale is equivalent to Bilawal thaat?

options.why: The minor scale has flattened 3rd, 6th and 7th degrees.

options.yes: Right! Bilawal with all shuddha notes maps to the major scale.

options.why: The pentatonic scale has only five notes.
The chromatic scale uses all 12 pitches.

questions.prompt: Which thaat uses komal Ga and komal Ni, giving a minor-like feel?
questions.no: It's Kafi thaat - its komal Ga and komal Ni give it a gentle, plaintive quality similar to the Western minor scale.

hints: Bilawal = all natural = major scale.
Kafi is mentioned in the content above - it flattens Ga and Ni.

tasks.title: Intervals and note relationships
content: Understanding the distance between notes helps you hear and play melodies accurately.

items: Sa to Pa is always a perfect fifth (7 semitones) - the strongest consonance after the octave
Sa to Ma is a perfect fourth (5 semitones)
Sa to Ga is a major third (4 semitones); Sa to komal Ga is a minor third (3 semitones)
Sa to Re is a major second (2 semitones); Sa to komal Re is a minor second (1 semitone)
Sa to upper Sa is an octave (12 semitones)

content: In Indian theory, the relationship between Sa and Pa is called 'samvadi' (consonant). Every raga has a 'vadi' (most important note) and a 'samvadi' (second most important), usually a fourth or fifth apart.

content.text: The vadi-samvadi relationship is what gives a raga its character. It is like the main character and supporting character of a story.

questions.prompt: How many semitones are between Sa and Pa?
questions.no: Sa to Pa is 7 semitones - a perfect fifth.

questions.prompt: What is the 'vadi' of a raga?

options.why: The first note is part of the raga's ascending pattern, not necessarily the vadi.

options.text: The most important note - the 'king' of the raga
options.yes: Right! The vadi is the note that gets the most emphasis and around which phrases revolve.

options.text: The highest note in the raga
options.why: The vadi can be any note in the raga's scale.

options.text: The note that is always played last
options.why: Ragas typically end on Sa, but the vadi is about emphasis, not position.

questions.prompt: If a raga's vadi is Re, its samvadi is most likely which note?

options.why: The samvadi is typically a fourth or fifth from the vadi.

options.yes: Right! Re to Pa is a perfect fourth - the typical vadi-samvadi relationship.

options.why: Sa is always important, but the samvadi is usually a fourth or fifth from the vadi.
The samvadi sits a fourth or fifth away, not a seventh.

hints: Count the semitones: S(0) r(1) R(2) g(3) G(4) m(5) M(6) P(7).
Vadi = king note, samvadi = minister note. They are usually a fourth or fifth apart.
Re to Pa: R(2) to P(7) = 5 semitones = a perfect fourth.
